page: Vultr vhf-12c-48gb is a High Frequency Compute server configured with 12 shared Intel x86_64 vCPUs, derived from 6 physical cores with hyper-threading. The system features 48.0 GB of system memory, providing 4.0 GB of RAM per core, and includes 768 GB of local NVMe SSD storage. It operates with a CPU clock speed of 2.0 GHz, supported by a cache hierarchy of 32 KB L1d, 4 MB L2, and 16 MB L3 cache.

Benchmark data indicates strong single-threaded performance, with gzip compression reaching top-tier status at 41.11 GB/sec and bzip3 decompression scoring in the top 25% at 14.55 GB/sec. Passmark memory testing also ranks in the top 10%. However, memory bandwidth for large uncached blocks is a notable bottleneck, falling into the bottom 25% for both read (33.97 GB/sec) and write (18.41 GB/sec) operations. Similarly, while small-model LLM inference is average, medium-model prompt processing and text generation are weak, scoring in the bottom 25%.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the server offers a high density of NVMe storage and memory relative to its shared CPU allocation. The shared CPU model introduces potential performance variability under sustained multi-tenant load, which is a key tradeoff. This configuration is suited for static web serving, database operations, and single-threaded compression tasks, but is less optimal for memory-bandwidth-intensive workloads or medium-to-large LLM inference.
description: Vultr vhf-12c-48gb is a High Frequency Compute server featuring 12 shared Intel x86_64 vCPUs, 48.0 GB of RAM, and 768 GB of local NVMe SSD storage. Operating at 2.0 GHz, the processor includes AVX, AES, and FMA instruction sets. Benchmark results show top-tier single-threaded gzip compression at 41.11 GB/sec and a top-10% Passmark memory score. However, performance tradeoffs exist, particularly in large-block memory bandwidth and medium-model LLM inference, both of which fall into the bottom 25%. The shared CPU allocation also introduces potential resource contention. This server is suited for static web serving, database operations, and general-purpose workloads requiring high local storage capacity, while workloads requiring sustained, uncached memory throughput or heavy AI inference should be avoided.
